newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-OPINION-Russell Barton's Canberra Closeup: Tax agenda.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-OPINION-Russell Barton's Canberra Closeup: Tax agenda.

text.p: By Russell Barton (ABC TV Political Editor)

A high-powered tax summit got under way in Canberra this morning with participants promoting everything from the Goods and Services Tax (GST) to flat income tax. But will there be a leading politician in sight?
Not on your life.
Coalition MPs are hamstrung by John Hewson's legacy -- the 1993 campaign promise that there will be no new taxes nor increases in existing taxes.
Like many other promises, that has been breached, notably the extra Medicare levy for higher income earners and the superannuation surcharge, also for those on more than A$75,000 a year.
Labor politicians have been bound by Kim Beazley's similar repudiation of consumption tax or, basically, any other discussion of tax.
Parliament can deal with all manner of sensitive subjects -- euthanasia, immigration, race, etc -- but it cannot talk sense on tax without great political cost.
That's why John Howard could not hide his delight on Tuesday when he received a transcript of Opposition Treasury spokesman Gareth Evans on Melbourne radio.
"I think since we are so under taxed by any relevant international standard there is a case for having some overall revenue increases," Evans said.
Howard said: "I think that statement is going to get a big run, Gareth, because basically what he is saying is that he believes in higher taxation."
On Wednesday he was as good as his word promising the voters of the western Sydney electorate of Lindsay that they face a clear choice at the October 19 by-election.
"If you vote Labor, you are voting for Gareth Evans' higher taxes," he said.

We would have heard a lot more of that had not the travelling Treasurer Peter Costello grabbed the limelight with his decision to brief reporters in Washington after his meeting with U.S. Federal Reserve Chairman, Alan Greenspan.
The Fed chief had told him he saw no threats to inflation, Costello said, adding that there was no expectation that U.S. interest rates would rise.
Two days of records for the Dow Jones index followed.
In fact a number of world markets shared the bullish tone Costello created.

But he managed also to turn damage control into damage creation by engaging in ludicrous denials of the briefing despite the fact he'd told reproters it was "on the record" and allowed them to tape his comments.
They immediately found their way onto the airwaves, giving the lie to his claims he had derived his views from reading the American newspapers.
But tax is not much safer ground for the coalition in the long run.
Ever since his re-election, Victorian premier Jeff Kennett has been almost daily banging the tax reform drum, his presentation progressively more strident.
This week it became such an urgent and vital need, Australia would fall into recession without it.
Yesterday the consequences of no action were "global by-pass."
John Howard was driven to offer the advice: "Jeff should take a holiday."
But Jeff is not about to back off.
He's now offering to help fund a tax inquiry if the federal parliament won't be in it.
And he's gaining support by the week.
Business groups are applauding his pressure, seeing him as a standard bearer and ice breaker.
It's increasingly clearer that the debate won't just conveniently die away until after the next election.
That's why both sides had better start working on a tax platform as soon as possible.
Howard can't hope that he can go to the poll still saying a GST is off the agenda.
No-one will believe that the coalition has no tax changes in mind if it is returned to office.
Similarly Labor won't be able to get away with mere sniping at the coalition.
Kim Beazley is using Kennett's campaign to raise questions about Howard's real intentions after the election.
But that won't suffice for long.
Labor should be positioning itself in the knowledge that the public will be expecting something more substantial than point-scoring.
That's sure to be fertilised by today's tax reform summit.
It will get wide coverage, helped by Kennett's preview pieces.
It's almost certain to fail to produce a definitive package due to its diverse make-up.

The joint sponsors, for instance -- the Australian Chamber of Commerce and Industry and the Australian Council of Social Service -- have widely divergent views on the importance of a broad-based consumption tax, for instance.
But the traversing of the options will generate more widespread knowledge of the deficiencies of the current system and more awareness of need for change.
(Views are those of the author, not those of Reuters)
-- Reuters Canberra Bureau 61-6 273 2730
